# Executive Summary

# Data and Exploratory Data Analysis {#initial-analysis}

In Part 1 we extracted and cleaned 15-minute discharge data from the River Don at Parkhill covering ten [water years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_year) (2016-2026). For Part 2, we have expanded this dataset to `r n_years` [water years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_year) (2001-2026). The threshold and independence criteria established in Part 1 are retained to identify extreme flow events with the quality codes reconsidered in Section \@ref(unchecked-readings) – \@ref(suspect-readings), and form the basis of our analysis of hydrograph shape uncertainty.

```{r tidyingthedata, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, tab.cap="Data used in this analysis, and the quality codes assigned to each reading"}
tidy_data_table
```

## Robson & Reed (1999) Independence Criteria Results

Having re-run our Part 1 analysis on the expanded dataset, we keep the threshold of `r u_final` $\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$ we established having obtained satisfactory results. We identified `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events across the `r n_years`-year observation period, corresponding to an average of `r sprintf("%.2f", nrow(peaks) / n_years)` events per year.

| Metric | Value | Unit |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Threshold (**$u$) | `r u_final` | $\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$ |
| **Total Independent Peaks** | `r nrow(peaks)` | events |
| **Average Peak Rate** | `r sprintf("%.2f", nrow(peaks) / n_years)` | peaks/year |
| **Period of Record** | `r n_years` | water years |

## Checking the data

Before constructing individual hydrographs for each extreme flow event, we assessed the reliability of the discharge readings for each of the `r nrow(peaks)` identified events. Each event was [initially represented using a common 120-hour window](#exploratory-analysis), extending `r win_before_h`` hours before and `r win_after_h` hours after its peak, with readings recorded at 15-minute intervals. For later analysis, we require all events to be [standardised](#standardising-the-hydrographs), forming the set of event windows used throughout the rest of the report.

In Part 1 we kept only Good (code 50) and Estimated (code 100) readings. Since Part 2 models the whole hydrograph of each event rather than only its peak, we reconsider the two groups of readings that were excluded: Unchecked readings (code 254), which we retain after the check below, and Suspect readings (code 150), which remain excluded.

### Unchecked readings {#unchecked-readings}

We identified `r nrow(unchecked_model$unique_readings)` Unchecked readings falling within `r n_distinct(unchecked_model$in_windows$Event_ID)` of the standardised event windows (Table \@ref(tab:uncheckeddata)).

```{r uncheckeddata, results="asis", echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(unchecked_model)) {
  knitr::kable(
    unchecked_model$table,
    format    = "markdown",
    align     = "llrrrrrr",
    col.names = c("Burst", "Event(s)", "Start", "Readings", "Duration (min)",
                  "Max flow (m³/s)", "RMSE (m³/s)", "Max abs. diff (m³/s)"),
    caption   = "Unchecked readings (code 254) within the event windows, compared with linear interpolation between the neighbouring checked readings."
  )
}
```

To fix this, we compared the original Unchecked readings with estimated values to decide whether retaining these Unchecked readings was reasonable. The estimated values were obtained by linear interpolation of the nearest checked readings by assuming a constant rate of change.

```{r uncheckedscatter, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Unchecked readings against the linear interpolation between neighbouring checked readings."}
if (!is.null(unchecked_model)) unchecked_model$plot
```

Figure \@ref(fig:uncheckedscatter) compares the Unchecked and interpolated values, with a dashed 1:1 line that represents perfect agreement. Since all Unchecked readings lie close to this line with a RMSE of `r sprintf("%.3f", unchecked_model$rmse)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ against discharge values of up to `r sprintf("%.0f", unchecked_model$max_q)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, these discrepancies are relatively small.

Although this does not prove that the Unchecked readings are completely accurate, the small size of the discrepancies provides some reassurance that retaining them is unlikely to significantly affect the hydrograph shapes.

Therefore, we retain the Unchecked SEPA readings rather than replacing them with the corresponding interpolated estimates as the values are close enough that preserving the original recorded values avoids unnecessary modification to the data.

### Suspect readings {#suspect-readings}

SEPA flags `r format(n_suspect, big.mark = ",")` readings (`r sprintf("%.2f", pct_suspect)`% of the record) as Suspect (code 150), meaning that the flow lies beyond the acceptable extrapolation limit of the gauge's stage-discharge relationship. As in Part 1, these readings are excluded. The largest Suspect reading is `r sprintf("%.1f", max_suspect)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, and `r n_suspect_above` exceed the threshold of `r u_final` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$. However, a reading below the threshold can still affect the shape of an event: wherever an excluded reading falls inside an event window, the hydrograph is linearly interpolated across the gap between the retained readings on either side. We therefore checked which Suspect readings fall inside the standardised event windows, using the same approach as for the Unchecked readings.

```{r suspecttext, results="asis", echo=FALSE}
if (is.null(suspect_model)) {
  cat("None of the Suspect readings fall inside any of the", nrow(events),
      "event windows, so excluding them does not affect any of the hydrographs we model.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "%d Suspect readings, in %d separate bursts, fall inside %d of the %d event windows (Table \\@ref(tab:suspectdata)). Figure \\@ref(fig:suspecthydro) shows where they lie within the hydrographs of the affected events, alongside the interpolated values the model uses in their place.\n",
    n_suspect_model_readings, n_suspect_model_bursts, n_suspect_model_events, nrow(events)))
}
```

```{r suspectdata, results="asis", echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(suspect_model)) {
  knitr::kable(
    suspect_model$table,
    format    = "markdown",
    align     = "llrrrrrr",
    col.names = c("Burst", "Event(s)", "Start", "Readings", "Duration (min)",
                  "Max flow (m³/s)", "RMSE (m³/s)", "Max abs. diff (m³/s)"),
    caption   = "Suspect readings (code 150) within the event windows. RMSE and maximum absolute difference compare each excluded reading with the linear interpolation used in its place."
  )
}
```

```{r suspecthydro, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Hydrographs of the events containing Suspect readings. The line shows the readings used in the model, which is the linear interpolation across each gap; points show the excluded Suspect readings; the dotted line is the threshold."}
if (!is.null(suspect_model_plot)) suspect_model_plot
```

## Exploratory Analysis {#exploratory-analysis}

To investigate the variation in hydrograph shape, the `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events are aligned at their maximum discharge, with the peak assigned time zero. Each hydrograph is examined over the same 120-hour window, allowing differences in peak magnitude, rising and falling behaviour to be compared.

```{r Hydrograph, echo=FALSE}
hydrograph_overlay_plot
```

Plotting all of the hydrographs on the same time scale shows the variation in shapes of extreme flow events. All events are aligned at their peaks showing not only do their maximum discharges differ considerably, (with the largest exceeding 400 $\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$) but the differences in the rate of discharge vary considerably.

Some events exhibit sharp peaks followed by rapid recession, whereas others have more broad hydrographs with gradual changes in discharge. Several events also display elevated discharge or secondary fluctuations away from the main peak, suggesting that extreme flow behaviour cannot always be accurately described by a single common shape.

While the mean hydrograph provides a useful summary of the typical event shape, it smooths over important differences between individual events. Consequently, representing every event using only an average hydrograph scaled by peak discharge may fail to capture the full variability in an event.

```{r heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.height=10, fig.width=9, fig.cap=cap_heatmap}
cap_heatmap <- paste0(
  "A heat map showing the variation in discharge and timeline of each of the ",
  nrow(peaks),
  " extreme flow events"
)
heat_map_plot
```

Figure \@ref(fig:heatmap), illustrates this variability further, with darker shading indicating higher discharge. The concentration of high discharge around time zero is expected as the hydrographs are aligned at their maximum flow. However, interestingly there is significant variation between events before and after their peak. In particular, some events maintain high discharge for longer periods, while others return to lower flows more rapidly.

Together, both these visualisations help illustrate the variation between event shapes not captured by only their maximum discharge.

## Standardising the hydrographs {#standardising-the-hydrographs}

From our analysis above we can see that extreme flow events differ in duration, peak discharge, and the relative timing of their peaks, so without standardisation, these differences would obscure the underlying variation in hydrograph shape.

To make the events comparable, each extreme flow event was first defined between its rising and falling limb troughs. Time was then rescaled to the interval [0,1], with zero representing the start of the event and one representing its end. The relative peak position was calculated as the time from the event start to its peak, divided by its total duration.

The rising and falling limbs were then rescaled separately so that every hydrograph reached its peak at the mean peak position across all events. This alignment allows differences in the shape of the rising and falling limbs to be compared without variation in peak timing dominating the analysis.

Discharge was also divided by the event's maximum flow, giving each standardised hydrograph a peak value of one. Finally, linear interpolation was used to represent every hydrograph at 64 equally spaced points on the standardised time scale.

The resulting data were arranged into a matrix (Y), with one row per extreme flow event and 64 columns representing common time points. This provides a consistent basis for comparing hydrograph shapes and applying the statistical modelling methods described in the following section.

Importantly, the original peak discharge, event duration and relative peak position are retained separately. These quantities allow fitted standardised hydrographs to be transformed back into physically meaningful discharge and time scales for subsequent model validation.

# Methods for representing hydrograph shape
The output of flood inundation models fit emulators. Since every input increases the number of runs to fit it, and each run is slow, we aim to minimise the number of inputs. After standardisation (Section \@ref{#standardising-the-hydrographs}), each of the ($N =$ `r nrow(Y)`) extreme flow events are summarised to `r n_grid` time points $u_j$, their standardised discharge $y_i(u_j)$, peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, duration $W_i$, and relative peak position $\tau_i$. 

Using all of these `r n_grid + 3` values as emulator inputs would be impractical. We therefore considered five methods for reducing the number of parameters needed to represent hydrograph shape. These methods are polynomial regression, principal component analysis (PCA), wavelets, B-splines and a gamma-type function. 

Most methods approximate each standardised hydrograph by a weighted sum of $K$ basis functions,

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_{ik}\,\phi_k(u),
(\#eq:basis)
\end{equation}

where $\phi_k(u)$ are the basis functions and $\theta_{ik}$ are the shape parameters for event $i$. The methods differ mainly in how these functions are chosen. Peak discharge, duration and relative peak position are retained separately, giving ($K+3$) parameters for each event. The exceptions are PCA, which first subtracts the mean curve before applying \@ref(eq:basis), and the gamma-type curve from our further reading, which is a nonlinear function of its parameters. 

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{x}_i = \left(Q_i^{\text{peak}},\; W_i,\; \tau_i,\; \boldsymbol{\theta}_i\right).
(\#eq:inputs)
\end{equation}

The emulator therefore only needs $3 + K$ inputs, where $K$ is significantly smaller than the previous `r n_grid`.

## SEPA's Approach {#method-SEPA}
SEPA's current approach is our baseline. It uses a fix-shape hydrograph, which is scaled according to maximum discharge. The baseline was constructed by averaging the standardised hydrographs (from \@ref{standardising-the-hydrographs}) without aligning their peaks, (as SEPA does not do so). The unaligned curves $\tilde{y}_i(u)$, are then averaged across extreme flow events,

\begin{equation}
\bar{y}(u) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{l=1}^{N} \tilde{y}_l(u),
(\#eq:sepa)
\end{equation}

and rescaled to have a peak value of one,

\begin{equation}
\hat{y}(u) = \frac{\bar{y}(u)}{\max_u \bar{y}(u)}.
(\#eq:sepa-2)
\end{equation}

The fitted hydrograph for extreme flow event $i$ is obtained by stretching $\hat{y}$ to the flood's duration $W_i$ and multiplying it by its peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$. This means every flood shares the same shape and differs only in its height and length. To test how well this shape predicts a flood it has not seen, each flood is also compared with the average of the other $N - 1$ floods only. 

Unlike SEPA's current approach, our baseline allows duration ($W_i$) to vary between events. This means the observed hydrographs now obtained may be more accurate than the strictly fixed-duration approach.

## Evaluation criteria {#methods-comparison}

Following the lectures, we evaluate each method on three criteria: accuracy, parsimony, and fitness for purpose. These are initially used to choose the number of parameters for each method (Sections 3.3-3.6) and then, to compare the methods at these choices and on common groundings (Section 5).

Since flood inundation uses real flows rather than standardised ones, we first convert each fitted curve back into a hydrograph in $m^3/s$ and hours by reversing the standardisation with each event's peak discharge, duration, and peak position. Then, we compare the fitted hydrograph $\hat{Q}_i(t)$ and the observed hydrograph $Q_i(t)$ for event $i$ at the same `r n_grid` time points, and summarise error by its average absolute value across all `r nrow(peaks)` extreme flow events.

**Accuracy:** We measure how closely the whole hydrograph is reproduced using the root mean squared error,

\begin{equation}
\text{RMSE}_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{`r n_grid`}\textstyle\sum_{j}\big(\hat{Q}_i(t_j) - Q_i(t_j)\big)^2}.
(\#eq:rmse)
\end{equation}

Where possible, the errors are calculated both within and out of sample. For methods whose basis or average shape is estimated from all extreme flow events together (SEPA's approach, PCA and the choice of wavelet coefficients), we use leave-one-out cross-validation, in which each event in turn is removed, the method is refitted to the remaining $N - 1$ events, and the removed event is predicted. For methods fitted to each event separately (polynomial, B-spline and gamma-type), leaving an event out does not change the fit to the others, so the in-sample and leave-one-out errors are identical; for these, the events were instead split once at random into `r length(train_floods)` training and `r length(test_floods)` test events, which is used to choose each method's number of parameters.

**Parsimony:** The number of parameters needed to achieve that accuracy matters because the parameters become the emulator's inputs, and fewer, less correlated parameters make both the emulator and the modelling of their uncertainty easier. We therefore compare the number of shape parameters of each method and the correlation between them across events.

**Fitness for purpose:** In addition to the RMSE, we also consider how well each method reproduces key hydrograph features,

\begin{align}
\text{Peak error}_i &= \max_j \hat{Q}_i(t_j) - \max_j Q_i(t_j), (\#eq:peak)\\
\text{Timing error}_i &= \hat{t}_{i}^{\,\text{peak}} - t_{i}^{\,\text{peak}}, (\#eq:timing)\\
\text{Volume error}_i &= 100 \times \frac{\int \hat{Q}_i(t)\,dt - \int Q_i(t)\,dt}{\int Q_i(t)\,dt}\ \%, (\#eq:volume)
\end{align}

where the integrals are evaluated by the trapezium rule. As every method except SEPA's places the peak at its observed position, their timing errors are close to zero by construction, so this error is mainly informative for the baseline. The second part of fitness for purpose, is how well unusual extreme flow events are reproduced, which we assess once their uncertainty has been modelled in Section \@ref(uncertainty).

## Polynomial regression {#method-polynomial}

First, we consider a polynomial in time as our choice of basis, so that the standardised hydrograph of event $i$ is approximated by

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \theta_{i1}u_j + \theta_{i2}u_j^2 + \dots + \theta_{ip}u_j^p, \qquad j = 1, \dots, `r n_grid`.
(\#eq:poly)
\end{equation}

Since this is a linear model, the coefficients are found by least squares as $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}_i$, where $X$ is the `r n_grid` $\times (p+1)$ matrix with columns $1, u, \dots, u^p$ evaluated at the grid times, and $\mathbf{y}_i$ is the standardised curve of event $i$. The $p + 1$ fitted coefficients are the shape parameters of the event.

To choose the degree $p$, we considered degrees from `r min(degrees)` to `r max(degrees)` in two ways. First, for each degree, we recorded the proportion of extreme flood events for which the highest-order term was significant at the 5% level (Table \@ref(tab:polysig)). Second, we compared the errors for each degree across the training and test floods (Section \@ref(methods-comparison), Figure \@ref(fig:polychoice)).

```{r polysig, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(degree = degrees, prop = sprintf("%.2f", prop_significant)),
  format    = "markdown",
  col.names = c("Degree $p$", "Proportion of events with $\\theta_p$ significant at 5%"),
  align     = "cc",
  caption   = "Proportion of events for which the highest-order polynomial term is significant at the 5% level."
)
```

```{r polychoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors for training and test events by polynomial degree."}
plot_choice(poly_choice, "Polynomial degree")
```

From Table \@ref(tab:polysig), we observe that the proportion of significant higher-order terms does not decrease steadily with the degree, but it is generally lower at even degrees than odd. However, we only use this table only as a guide, because neighbouring points on a hydrograph are strongly correlated, which violates the independence assumption of the linear model, producing overly-optimistic results since standard errors are small.

Hence, we primarily choose the order from Figure \@ref(fig:polychoice), where we observe that all four errors fall as the degree increases, and the test errors follow training errors closely. Also, we see a similar even-odd trend from Table 3 across all four errors, with the largest improvements occuring when moving to a higher odd degree. The step from degree 6 to 7 is among the largest reductions in peak error, RMSE and timing error, with volume error staying approximately the same. Across all four errors, further increases either see a leveling off after degree 7, or smaller gains for each additional parameter, meaning degree 8 gives similar errors. Therefore, we choose $p =$ `r p_chosen`.

## Principal component analysis {#method-pca}

Unlike the polynomial, where the basis is fixed before looking at the data, PCA estimates the basis from the extreme flow events themselves, finding the curves that best describe how the events differ from one another. To do this, we arrange the standardised hydrographs into the `r nrow(Y)` $\times$ `r n_grid` matrix $Y$, with one row per event, and centre each column by subtracting the mean curve $\bar{y}(u_j)$. We do not scale the columns, as every column is already on the same standardised scale. PCA then finds the principal components $\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots$, which are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix of $Y$, ordered so that the first explains the most variation between events, the second the most of what remains, and so on. Each standardised hydrograph is then approximated by

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \bar{y}(u_j) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \xi_{ik}\,\phi_k(u_j), \qquad \xi_{ik} = \sum_{j=1}^{`r n_grid`} \big(y_i(u_j) - \bar{y}(u_j)\big)\,\phi_k(u_j),
(\#eq:pca)
\end{equation}

where the scores $\xi_{i1}, \dots, \xi_{iK}$ are the shape parameters of event $i$. An advantage of PCA is that the scores of different components are uncorrelated across events by construction, which makes their variation between events easier to model.

```{r pcaloadings, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="The first three principal components against standardised time."}
matplot(grid_u, pca_result$rotation[, 1:3], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"),
        xlab = "Standardised time u", ylab = "Loading", main = "")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"), bty = "n")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:pcaloadings) shows the first three principal components, which together explain `r round(100 * cum_var[3])`% of the variation between events. We observe that all three are close to zero at the peak, $u^\ast =$ `r round(u_star, 2)`, since every standardised hydrograph has the same value there. The first component, which alone explains `r round(100 * cum_var[1])`% of the variation, has the same sign on both sides of the peak, and so describes how broad the event is, that is, how high the flow stays relative to the peak, particularly on the rising limb. The second component has opposite signs before and after the peak, and so contrasts the flow shortly before the peak with the flow during the recession. The third component is concentrated on the rising limb, and describes how late and how steeply the flow rises towards the peak, which also captures events with an earlier, smaller peak.

To choose the number of components $K$, we again considered two approaches. First, we plotted the cumulative proportion of the variation explained against $K$ (Figure \@ref(fig:pcacumvar)), where the common rule of explaining 95% of the variation gives $K =$ `r which(cum_var >= 0.95)[1]`. Second, since the components are estimated from all events together, we compared the in-sample and leave-one-out errors for each $K$ (Section \@ref(methods-comparison), Figure \@ref(fig:pcachoice)), recalculating the mean curve and components without each left-out event before reconstructing it. We observe that the RMSE and volume error fall as $K$ increases, with the leave-one-out errors only slightly above the in-sample errors, so the components found from the other events generalise well to a new event. Moving from 6 to 7 components gives almost no improvement in the leave-one-out RMSE, so, in agreement with the 95% rule, we chose $K =$ `r k_chosen`. We also observe that the peak and timing errors are very small for every $K$, at under 1 m³/s and 1 hour, since the variation between events at the peak is almost zero, so the mean curve already reproduces the peak.

```{r pcacumvar, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Cumulative proportion of variation explained by the first $K$ principal components, with the dashed line at 95%."}
plot(seq_along(cum_var), cum_var, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of components K", ylab = "Cumulative proportion of variation")
abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2, col = "#AA1945")
```

```{r pcachoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors, in-sample and leave-one-out, by number of principal components."}
plot_choice(pca_choice, "Number of components K")
```

## Wavelets {#method-wavelets}

Finally, we consider wavelets. A wavelet is a short, localised wave that starts at zero, oscillates briefly and returns to zero, and a hydrograph can be built up from shifted and stretched copies of a single wavelet, each describing the detail in the curve at a particular time and scale. This makes wavelets potentially well suited to hydrographs, which are often dominated by a single sharp peak that may be described by only a few of them. As for the polynomial, the basis is fixed and fitted to each extreme flow event separately, but here using wavelet functions in place of powers of time.

Using the discrete wavelet transform, each standardised hydrograph is split into a smooth trend and the detail at `r wav_levels` successively coarser scales, so that

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) = \sum_{k} a_{ik}\,\varphi_k(u) + \sum_{j=1}^{`r wav_levels`}\sum_{k} d_{ijk}\,\psi_{jk}(u),
(\#eq:wavelet)
\end{equation}

where the $a_{ik}$ are the smooth coefficients, describing the overall shape of the hydrograph, and the $d_{ijk}$ are the detail coefficients at scale $j$ and location $k$, with $j = 1$ the finest scale. We used the Daubechies wavelet with four coefficients, `r wav_levels` levels and periodic boundaries, and since `r n_grid` $= 2^6$, the transform can be applied to each hydrograph directly. With these settings, each hydrograph has `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth coefficients and `r n_grid - n_grid / 2^wav_levels` detail coefficients, so that using all of them would reproduce the hydrograph exactly. Figure \@ref(fig:wavdecomp) shows this decomposition for event 1, where we observe that the smooth coefficients capture the overall shape of the event, while the detail coefficients are close to zero except around the peak, and are smallest at the finest scale.

```{r wavdecomp, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Wavelet decomposition of event 1: the detail coefficients at each level and the smooth coefficients."}
par(mfrow = c(4, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 2, 1))
plot(wt_example@W[[1]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 1 detail (finest)")
plot(wt_example@W[[2]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 2 detail")
plot(wt_example@W[[3]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 3 detail (coarsest)")
plot(wt_example@V[[3]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#174B67", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 3 smooth")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

To reduce the number of parameters, we keep all of the smooth coefficients but only the $M$ detail coefficients that are largest on average across events, setting the rest to zero. The same $M$ coefficients are kept for every event, so that all events share the same basis, and the shape parameters of each event are its `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth coefficients and $M$ kept detail coefficients. To choose $M$, we compared the in-sample and leave-one-out errors for different values of $M$ (Section \@ref(methods-comparison), Figure \@ref(fig:wavchoice)), where for each left-out event the coefficients to keep are chosen from the remaining events only. We observe that the leave-one-out errors are almost identical to the in-sample errors, since leaving out one event barely changes which coefficients are largest on average. The peak error falls sharply up to $M = 5$ and then stays roughly constant up to $M = 10$, while the RMSE continues to fall more gradually and the volume error stays below 0.25% throughout. Since each additional coefficient adds a parameter, we chose $M =$ `r keep_chosen`, giving `r ncol(wav_params)` shape parameters per event.

```{r wavchoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors, in-sample and leave-one-out, by number of detail coefficients kept."}
plot_choice(wav_choice, "Detail coefficients kept")
```

We also checked the sensitivity of the results to the choice of wavelet and the number of levels, keeping $M =$ `r keep_chosen` fixed (Table \@ref(tab:wavsens)). Since more levels give fewer smooth coefficients, this also changes the number of parameters. We observe that the number of levels matters much more than the choice of wavelet, with the RMSE, peak and volume errors all increasing as the number of levels increases and the number of parameters falls, from 13 parameters at three levels to 7 at five levels. For a given number of levels, the `haar` wavelet has a noticeably higher RMSE than the two Daubechies wavelets. The least asymmetric Daubechies wavelet with eight coefficients, `la8`, has a similar RMSE to `d4`, and a lower peak error at three levels (`r sprintf("%.2f", wav_sensitivity$peak_error[wav_sensitivity$filter == "la8" & wav_sensitivity$levels == 3])` compared with `r sprintf("%.2f", wav_sensitivity$peak_error[wav_sensitivity$filter == "d4" & wav_sensitivity$levels == 3])` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$). Given the `la8` wavelet has the lowest average absolute errors across the board at three levels, we select it.

```{r wavsens, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  wav_sensitivity, digits = 2, format = "markdown",
  col.names = c("Wavelet", "Levels", "Shape parameters", "RMSE (m³/s)",
                "Peak error (m³/s)", "Timing error (h)", "Volume error (%)"),
  caption = "Average absolute errors for different wavelets and numbers of levels, keeping the same number of detail coefficients."
)
```

## Other methods {#method-other}

As well as the three methods suggested in the lectures, we considered two further methods, each addressing a weakness found above.

### B-splines {#method-bspline}

The polynomial's weaknesses all stem from using a single curve across the whole event, so we also considered a B-spline basis, which joins short cubic pieces smoothly together so that each basis function only affects one part of the hydrograph (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005). The standardised hydrograph is approximated by $y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \theta_{il}\,B_l(u_j)$, where $B_1, \dots, B_L$ are cubic B-splines with equally spaced knots, and it is fitted and validated in the same way as the polynomial. We chose $L =$ `r n_basis_chosen`, giving `r n_basis_chosen + 1` shape parameters, close to the `r p_chosen + 1` of the polynomial, so that the two can be compared at a similar number of parameters.

### A known hydrograph function {#method-gamma}

The lectures suggest that a known function which approximates hydrographs may give parameters that can be interpreted. We therefore fitted a gamma-type hydrograph (Nash, 1957) with an added baseflow to each extreme flow event by nonlinear least squares, giving three parameters with a physical meaning: the baseflow as a fraction of the peak flow (median `r sprintf("%.2f", median(gamma_params[gamma_ok, "b"]))`), the time of the peak, and the sharpness of the peak.

# Validation of methods

We now validate the methods at their chosen number of parameters.


## Contrasting extreme flow events {#validation-contrast}

```{r all-methods-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 10, fig.cap = "Observed (black) and fitted curves from each method for six contrasting floods: earliest peak (event 2), latest peak (41), shortest (26), longest (19), flattest (29) and sharpest (3)."}
plot_all_methods()
```

The polynomial method underestimates sharp peaks and cannot reproduce multi-peak extreme flow events (Figure \@ref(fig:all-methods-plot)), instead fitting a single peak that is too low and broad. This is because each term acts over the whole event, so a sharp change at the peak would disrupt the rest of the curve, while the higher-order terms dominate near the ends, causing the fit to drift away from the observed flow there. The B-spline method fits the recession and ends closely, but shows the same pattern around the peak, with only a marginal improvement on multi-peak events. The gamma-type method performs the poorest, as each curve has a single peak and the same baseflow at the start and end, fitting the peaks and ends of contrasting extreme flow events poorly.

Unlike these three methods, PCA reproduces single-peak events almost exactly and multi-peak events closely. For multi-peak events, PCA tends to underestimate at least one of the smaller peaks.

The wavelet method performs similarly to PCA. However, its curves are jagged in places with unrealistic dips, which we expect is because the same detail coefficients are kept for every flood. Additionally, there are sharp deviations at the ends, likely due to the periodic boundary.

## Residuals

```{r residuals-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Residuals against rescaled time for each method (grey: individual floods; coloured: average), with the five averages compared in the final panel."}
plot_all_residuals()
```

The residuals (Figure \@ref(fig:residuals-all)) confirm these observations across all extreme flow events. The polynomial residuals are positive at the peak and negative on either side for most, confirming that the fitted peak is systematically too low and broad, while the B-spline residuals are similar around the peak but close to zero after $u \approx 0.6$. The gamma-type method has the widest spread. On the other hand, the residuals for PCA are small throughout, largest on the rising limb, and the average is exactly zero by construction. The wavelet method also has small residuals throughout, with a jagged average. 

Neighbouring residuals are correlated, so the independence assumed by the regression-based methods does not hold, but this does not affect their use here, as the fitted curves are used as a basis rather than for inference.

## Correlation of parameters

Finally, the polynomial coefficients are strongly correlated across events, from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(abs(cor(poly_coefs)[upper.tri(cor(poly_coefs))])))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cor(poly_coefs)[upper.tri(cor(poly_coefs))])))` in absolute value, because the powers of $u$ are highly correlated on the interval. The correlations are weaker for the B-spline coefficients, up to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cor(bspline_coefs)[upper.tri(cor(bspline_coefs))])))`, and the wavelet parameters, from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(abs(cor(wav_params)[upper.tri(cor(wav_params))])))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cor(wav_params)[upper.tri(cor(wav_params))])))`, with the strongest between neighbouring smooth coefficients, and mostly weaker correlations between smooth and detail coefficients. Unlike these methods, the PCA scores are uncorrelated by construction, and the gamma-type parameters are only weakly correlated, up to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cor(gamma_params[gamma_ok, ])[upper.tri(cor(gamma_params[gamma_ok, ]))])))`. This matters because simulating new extreme flow events requires a joint distribution for the shape parameters, and every correlation must be estimated from only 41 events, which favours PCA for the uncertainty analysis in Section \@ref(uncertainty).

# Uncertainty analysis {#uncertainty}

We explored three kinds of uncertainty in Lecture 3: parametric uncertainty, function uncertainty, and structural discrepancy. Function uncertainty and structural discrepancy both relate to the emulator, so we explore them in \@ref{emulator}, and here we focus on parametric uncertainty in $\mathbf{x_i}$.

Points close to the black line indicate an approximately Normal parameter."}
plot_all_qq()
```

## Other uncertainties (sampling in code while reconstruction, peak detection and cleaning choices and any others from lecture 5 final slide to be explored in words)

```{r sampling-bands, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Sampling uncertainty: lower (blue) and upper (red) edges of the simulated 90\\% band from 100 refits to resampled sets of floods, with the band from all 41 floods in black."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (method in names(bootstrap_bands)) {
  bands <- bootstrap_bands[[method]]
  matplot(grid_u, t(rbind(bands$lower, bands$upper)), type = "l", lty = 1,
          col = c(rep(adjustcolor("#5298BC", 0.2), n_boot),
                  rep(adjustcolor("#AA1945", 0.2), n_boot)),
          xlab = "Rescaled time u", ylab = "Flow / peak flow",
          main = paste0(method, ": 90% band, ", n_boot, " refits"))
  lines(grid_u, apply(full_band[[method]], 2, quantile, probs = 0.05), lwd = 2)
  lines(grid_u, apply(full_band[[method]], 2, quantile, probs = 0.95), lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r sampling-table, echo = FALSE}

rownames(sampling_table) <- c("Average width of the 90\\% band",

      caption = "Sampling uncertainty, as fractions of the peak flow averaged over the curve. Small variation of the band edges compared with the band width means sampling error is a small part of the overall uncertainty.")
```

- e.g, explain the two separate phases,

First, SEPA could select different parameter combinations, reconstruct corresponding hydrographs and run these through the actual flood inundation model. The resulting input-output pairs would be used to train an emulator.

Second, SEPA could repeatedly sample parameters from your fitted uncertainty distribution and feed those parameters into the trained emulator to obtain a distribution of predicted extreme flow event outcomes.
